original_value: AbstractBackgroundOur current understanding of archaic admixture in humans relies on statistical methods with large biases, whose magnitudes depend on the sizes and separation times of ancestral populations. To avoid these biases, it is necessary to estimate these parameters simultaneously with those describing admixture. Genetic estimates of population histories also confront problems of statistical identifiability: different models or different combinations of parameter values may fit the data equally well. To deal with this problem, we need methods of model selection and model averaging, which are lacking from most existing software.ResultsThe Legofit software package allows simultaneous estimation of parameters describing admixture, and the sizes and separation times of ancestral populations. It includes facilities for data manipulation, estimation, analysis of residuals, model selection, and model averaging.ConclusionsLegofit uses genetic data to study the history of a subdivided population. It is unaffected by recent history and can therefore focus on the deep history of population size, subdivision, and admixture. It outperforms several statistical methods that have been widely used to study population history and should be useful in any species for which DNA sequence data is available from several populations.

result.paraphrase: AbstractBackgroundOur current understanding of archaic admixture in humans depends on statistical approaches with substantial bias, and the size of that bias is influenced by ancestral population sizes and their split times. To avoid these biases, those parameters must be estimated at the same time as the admixture parameters. Genetic reconstruction of population history also faces statistical identifiability issues, where different models or parameter combinations can explain the data equally well. Addressing this requires model selection and model averaging methods, which are missing from most existing software.ResultsThe Legofit software package enables simultaneous estimation of admixture parameters along with ancestral population sizes and separation times. It provides tools for data manipulation, estimation, residual analysis, model selection, and model averaging.ConclusionsLegofit uses genetic data to infer the history of a subdivided population. Because it is unaffected by recent history, it can concentrate on the deep history of population size, subdivision, and admixture. It performs better than several widely used statistical methods for studying population history and should be useful for any species with DNA sequence data from multiple populations.
